newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japanese house wins Soon Soon corn/beans tender.
newsitem.headline: Japanese house wins Soon Soon corn/beans tender.

text.p: A Japanese trading house won the bidding for a combined cargo of 55,000 tonnes of soybeans and corn in a tender by Malaysia's Soon Soon Oilmills Sdn Bhd, traders said on Thursday.
"The Japanese house won," a senior trader for a commodity company in Singapore said.

"That's correct, a Japanese trade house won the deal," a dealer for a commodity firm here said. "There were three of them involved in the bidding. I think the winner submitted a bid a few dollars below the market rate."
The name of the winners were not immediately available but Marubeni and Mitsui were said to have taken part in the tender.
The shipment is for November arrival.
Traders said Soon Soon would normally buy a combination cargo of 30,000 tonnes of soybeans and 25,000 tonnes of corn.
The likely price of the winning bid, dealers said, would be a few dollars below US$134-$136 a tonne C&F for corn and around $330-$332 a tonne C&F for soybeans.
"I was not surprised a Japanese house won the tender. The Japanese are very aggressive in giving discounts to people like Soon Soon," one trader said.
Traders said the interest in the tender result among regional dealers was due to the fact that there was very little spot business being concluded in Southeast Asia.

"There are bits and pieces here and there, but it's very, very quiet. The only ones I saw in the market recently were the South Koreans picking up corn. In this region, everybody has coverage and that's why corn prices are slumping," one said.
U.S. corn coming into Southeast Asia was seen by the trade at around $136-$138 a tonne C&F for July/August shipment on a Panamax against last week's quote of $140-$142 a tonne C&F.
Chinese corn in Southeast Asia was quoted at between $137-$139 a tonne C&F for July/August shipment mainly on a Handy against $135-$137 last week.
Argentine corn was already out of the picture with a quote of $140-$143 a tonne C&F on a Panamax for July/August shipment.
"Argentine corn is no longer workable. It's more or less gone," one dealer said. "The trade is going back to U.S. origins."
Dealers were also paying more attention to open positions from August onwards in Indonesia, which they estimate will need to buy between 50,000 to 90,000 tonnes of soymeal.
Malaysia may be open for 20,000 tonnes of soymeal in September while Thailand was said to be looking for at least a Handy-sized vessel of soymeal for forward delivery.
"Indonesia does have open positions in August for soymeal. But August is still far away and they are not in any hurry to buy," a dealer said.

"People here know the market. They know that prices will still come off in Chicago. They'd rather wait for more bearish USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) numbers to knock the soy prices down," another dealer said.
Regional dealers shrugged off worries over the possible impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon on crops across the Asia-Pacific region.
"Any impact by El Nino is for later this year. It's too early and I'll worry about it as we get closer to the end of the year," one dealer said.

The El Nino, named for the Christ child by Peruvian anchovy fishermen who noted its appearance around Christmas, comes from a warm ocean current appearing off the South American coast in the Pacific ocean.
It plays havoc with normal weather patterns around the world and the most severe in recent memory in 1983 caused withering drought in Indonesia, the Philippines, Australia and South Africa.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
